study.title: Formation and Detectability of PSR J0653+0443-like Extremely Eccentric Binary Neutron Stars in the Milky Way

cover.headline: A new model suggests **extremely lopsided neutron star orbits** may not be as rare as they first seemed.

slides.title: When you find one of something bizarre, you cannot tell if you got lucky or if there are thousands.
slides.body:
A survey found neutron stars in the most eccentric orbit ever seen. The team reports that such extreme systems could make up a small but real slice of the galaxy's population.

That means detection was not a fluke. These orbits may follow naturally from how neutron stars form.

slides.title: The team modeled how many neutron star pairs with eccentricity above 0.99 a full sky survey should detect.
slides.body:
Their calculations suggest systems that eccentric account for roughly 0.6 percent of what the survey can see. They predict around 0.31 detections across the full footprint.

The completed survey has about a 15 percent chance of finding another above 0.99.

slides.title: PSR J0653+0443 has an orbital eccentricity of 0.992, the highest known in the Milky Way.
slides.body:
Eccentricity measures how stretched an orbit is. A circle is zero, and these neutron stars come within a hair of a straight line.

Before this model, it was unclear whether standard binary evolution could produce something so extreme.

caveats: This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed yet, so no independent expert has checked the work.
This is a model, not a direct measurement. The numbers depend on assumptions about how binary stars evolve and how surveys find pulsars.
This study found a pattern, not a cause. Something else could explain the link between formation pathways and eccentricity.

source.abstract: Recently, the Five-hundred-meter-Aperture-Spherical-radio-Telescope (FAST) Galactic Plane Pulsar Snapshot (GPPS) survey discovers an extraordinary binary neutron star (BNS) system, PSR J0653+0443, possessing the highest known orbital eccentricity ($e\approx0.992$) among Galactic BNSs (Yang et al., 2026), which provides a unique probe into the formation and evolution of BNSs. In this Letter, we perform compact binary population synthesis calculations with self-consistent neutron star spin evolution to model extremely eccentric BNS population detectable by the FAST GPPS survey, explicitly incorporating observational selection effects. We find that BNSs with $e>0.99$ constitute only $\sim0.6\%$ of the detectable population, with an expected detection number of $λ_{\mathrm{GPPS}}\approx0.31$ over the full planned footprint. Thus, although rare, systems as eccentric as PSR J0653+0443 are compatible with standard binary evolution. We further demonstrate that extremely eccentric BNSs arise preferentially from core-collapse supernovae, whereas imposing $P\lesssim0.1$ s select older, more frequently recycled systems, which naturally reproduce the observed properties of PSR J0653+0443. We further predict that the completed GPPS sample has a $\sim15\%$ chance of finding another $e>0.99$ BNS, but a much higher $\sim88\%$ chance for $e>0.90$ systems. By contrast, future facilities are expected to enlarge the detectable highly eccentric BNS population, with SKA potentially detecting PSR J0653+0443-like systems and sub-mHz gravitational-wave detectors probing a larger population with $e>0.9$, enabling much more in-depth population-level constraints.
